title: Warmup Convergence Notes — swapbench trace experiments
content:
Goal:
- Quick notes and raw numbers from the swapbench warmup convergence experiments (mix of synthetic traces + captured prod-sample). Trying to capture: how many requests until p95/p99 stabilizes, how different pool eviction behaviours affect steady-state, and whether we can detect an "elbow" in latency vs. hit-rate that predicts convergence time.

Environment:
- Cluster: dedicated dev cluster (2x A100-40GB per node), 6 nodes used for this run.
- Binary: runtime v0.62.3-swapbench (small patch: kv-cache eviction TTL jitter disabled).
- Model: llama-7b-fp16-optimized (seq=1024), batcher: adaptive-0.5, max-batch=64.
- Workload generators: custom swapbench harness (attached in GH link), plus a harvested sample trace from prod (hour window, anonymized).

Experiment designs (three variants):
1) Steady ramp: linear ramp from 10 qps -> 800 qps over 15m, then hold 30m.
2) Swapbench alternating: 5m cold burst (new unique prefixes) -> 10m warm period (repeats prefixes) -> repeat 6x. This mimics tenant churn and model cache churn.
3) Fingerprint stress: constant 300 qps but each request flips a single byte in prefix (low reuse but similar size) to exercise KV cache collision behaviour.

Key metrics captured per 10s window:
- qps, inflight, mean latency, p50/p95/p99, kv-cache hit rate, GPU utilization, avg tokens/sec per GPU, tail spike count (# windows where p99 > 2x baseline).

Raw observations (high level):
- Steady ramp: p95 rises smoothly during ramp and then settles after ~6m of stable load. Convergence (p95 within 10% of steady median) took ~6.5m after the ramp plateau. KV-hit reached 82% at convergence.
- Swapbench alternating: each cold burst produced large p99 spikes that decayed exponentially but did not fully return to previous baseline before next cold burst started when the period < 7m. With 5m cold bursts we saw cumulative degradation: baseline p95 increased by ~18% after 3 cycles.
- Fingerprint stress: KV hit stayed ~8–12% and latency was stable but higher (p95 ~1.9x of baseline). GPU utilization lower than steady-ramp (more CPU/KV pressure).

Detailed numbers (representative windows):
- Steady ramp: at plateau (800 qps): p50=62ms, p95=210ms, p99=540ms, kv-hit=82%, GPU util=78%
- After first cold swap (swapbench): immediate p99 jump to 1.8s for 30s window, average tokens/sec dropped 24%, CPU loops for cache reconciliation spiked.
- Swapbench cumulative: baseline p95 before cycles = 200ms; after 4 cycles = 236ms (18% incr).

Hypotheses / interpretations:
- Convergence is not only a function of requests count but of unique-prefix entropy. If unique-prefix rate per sec > cache ingestion throughput, convergence will never reach the same hit-rate.
- There is an operational "memory": short periods (<7m) of churn cause additive residuals because eviction + re-population creates thrash.
- Fingerprint stress shows that when cache hit-rate is low the bottleneck shifts from GPU to CPU/IO path; batching buys less when reuse is low.

Quick checks / sanity rules to add to platform heuristics:
- If observed unique-prefix rate > 40% of reqs for 3 consecutive minutes, trigger slow-path pre-warm (speculative KV insert) to reduce p99 spikes.
- If p99 spikes > 3x baseline more than twice in 10 minutes, automatically widen batch timeout by +10ms for next 5 minutes to improve throughput vs tail penalty.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Repeat runs using smaller models (3B) and larger sequence lengths (2048) — does convergence timeline scale linearly? (hypothesis: longer seq increases kernel variance and amplifies tail).
- Instrumentation: capture per-request KV-lookup latency distribution (not just hit rate). Current metrics are aggregate and hide heavy-tail lookups.
- Try prefetch experiment: when prefix seen N times in short window, proactively pin to hotpool for T minutes. Measure whether pinning reduces p99 without increasing eviction churn.
- Replay prod-sample under variant where we limit cache population rate to 50% of measured to see effect of slower ingestion.

Notes on methodology and gotchas:
- Make sure harness does not reuse connection-level caches (we used new http connections per worker to avoid client-side reordering).
- Warmup windows are sensitive to generator seeding; keep seeds in GH run artifacts.
- Single-run numbers are noisy; need 3 replicates (we have 2 so far). Running final replicate next week.

Quick final takeaways (for deck):
- Warmup convergence has an "elbow" behavior gated by unique-prefix churn rate; low-churn workloads converge in minutes, medium-churn needs tens of minutes, high-churn may not converge without additional pre-warming or pinning.
- Operational knobs (speculative insert, adaptive batch timeout) show promise in simulations and should be A/B tested on a small fleet.

Scratch TODO (practical):
- [ ] Add per-request kv-lookup histogram to telemetry (instrumentation PR).
- [ ] Run 3rd replicate for Swapbench variant and attach raw CSV.
- [ ] Draft proposal for pre-warm/pinning experiment and hardware cost estimate.

Misc raw links / references:
- swapbench harness: GH link above (GH: redwood-inference/swapbench#142)
- related prod-incident: SERV-812 (cold-surge on Europe region)

End of notes — these are raw; will tidy for postmortem if we A/B test a mitigation.

-- Niko
